title: Brokeback Mountain (2005): a masterpiece of the 2000s

commenti.body: Ennis only allowing himself to be gay in a campsite far away from society..so heartbreaking but realistic. I think the soundtrack and story go together in this movie better than almost any other movie has ever done.

I’m a gay man, born in the 1960’s. Yeah, it’s kind of a milestone, and not the “old tragic formula.” That old formula showed gay men as sexless funny neighbors. And if they were portrayed as sexual beings, they were punished in the end with death or a tragedy of some sort. Brokeback showed true, long-lasting love between 2 men, and the “bad guy” in the story is the society that demands that they hide their love from the world. While the story ends tragically, it’s not a punishment of the characters, it’s an indictment of the society that damns Jack to endure that pain alone. For a whole lot of gay men, it was a story that they knew very well, but had never seen portrayed in a movie. If you aren’t gay, it might be hard to appreciate how life-changing that movie was.

Oh my gosh, this is a wonderfully insightful reading of the film regarding Christianity and the imagery of the Shepards. I have not considered this - I wasn’t aware of the Pentecostal perspective!

I personally could talk about this movie forever.
In particular your point about Brokeback being  away from civilisation. 

This is one of my favourite story-telling tropes, much like Shakespeare’s As you like it, in which the characters leave the city and enter a forest where they get to play with their identities and find love.  

Often I think the film gets painted as an “old tragic formula” without recognising the story is about homophobia and how it impacts the human spirit, not just in the lives of Ennis and Jack but of the people around them. It is a tragedy on purpose, rooted in the culture and attitudes of a specific time and place. 

And in my opinion does it exceptionally well. I watched it when it came out and was a teenager, so when I do watch it again I pick up on all the subtle ways the story builds stakes. The story Ennis tells Jack, of the man who was murdered and left on display as a warning. How his father “made sure (he’d) seen it”. Because they aren’t just fearing God, they are fearing the punishment of man. Especially Ennis. It’s in my opinion the moment in that man’s life that dictates all his actions. 

I think it should 100% be considered an important American film. Not just for its depiction of romantic love between men, but on a technical level it tells that story in an incredibly delicate and skilful way.

"Jack, I swear."

Never been quite so gutted by a movie.

It's a great film marred by pretty much one thing, how unrealistically young the leads look when they're supposed to be past their prime, defeated 40 somethings with no hope for a future. Anne Hathaway is straight up miscast though, her and her accent and her stupid blonde wig looking like a vapid teenager at the end of the movie is just a black mark on the production. A masterpiece otherwise.

Thank you for your comment! Most of the people I've talked to about the film, including myself, were born in the 1990s, so we didn't experience the period depicted in the movie firsthand. Reading your account was definitely enlightening. Despite all its sad and tragic elements, I like to think the film has a beautifully happy ending, with Ennis opening up to the world and to relationships with others.

Thank you so much for your comment! I also watched the film for the first time when I was a teenager. Although it had a profound impact on me at that time, I only managed to reflect on other aspects of it as I revisited the film over the years.

Ang Lee's direction is definitely a standout. The way he captures nature is simply superb (and it greatly reinforces the nature vs. civilization contrast you mentioned, starting with the first scene where Jack's big truck is just a tiny speck against the vastness of the mountains). Do you think we can consider it his best work in the English language?

And yes, the fake sideburns—and also Anne Hathaway's wigs—are quite laughable.

"Brokeback Mountain" and the final episode of "Six Feet Under" were both released in 2005, and they are two of my favorite works in the history of visual storytelling. Another thing they have in common is that, despite being magnificently written and directed, the aging makeup and wigs used on the actors are simply awful, giving a comedic touch to moments that were definitely intended to be very dramatic.

It's maybe my favorite movie ever? I've seen it soo many times and each time it deepens my appreciation for how beautifully it tells its story. I love the characters, the cinematography, the script. It's just perfect. Great analysis!

> Six Feet Under
